original_value: Modern introductory courses on AI do not train students to create intelligent systems or provide broad coverage of this complex field. In this paper, we identify problems with common approaches to teaching artificial intelligence and suggest alternative principles that courses should adopt instead. We illustrate these principles in a proposed course that teaches students not only about component methods, such as pattern matching and decision making, but also about their combination into higher-level abilities for reasoning, sequential control, plan generation, and integrated intelligent agents. We also present a curriculum that instantiates this organization, including sample programming exercises and a project that requires system integration. Participants also gain experience building knowledge-based agents that use their software to produce intelligent behavior.

result.paraphrase: Modern introductory AI courses do not teach students to build intelligent systems or give broad coverage of this intricate field. This paper examines shortcomings in standard approaches to teaching artificial intelligence and proposes alternative principles that courses should follow. It demonstrates these principles through a proposed course that covers component methods like pattern matching and decision making, as well as how they combine into higher-level capabilities for reasoning, sequential control, plan generation, and integrated intelligent agents. A curriculum implementing this structure is also presented, with sample programming exercises and a project requiring system integration. Participants likewise gain hands-on experience creating knowledge-based agents that use software to generate intelligent behavior.
